domain: Why 'follow your heart' advice about choosing a life partner is right, even though almost every argument given for it is wrong
topic: Why 'follow your heart' advice about choosing a life partner is right, even though almost every argument given for it is wrong

movement.gist: Stage the popular romantic wisdom in full voice: trust your gut about a partner, chemistry doesn't lie, the people who overthink compatibility with checklists and questionnaires end up divorced while the ones who 'just knew' stay together — narrated through the folklore of engagement stories, dating-app skeptics, relatives who married after three weeks.

Separate the conclusion (feeling-based choice tends to work) from its bad arguments (that feeling is a hidden compatibility-scanner, that instinct evolved to detect the right person) — casually drop, as if in passing, that the advice can be right while every folk explanation for why it's right is false.

State plainly that people who choose on feeling do seem to fare about as well, often better, than those who choose by criteria-matching — preserve this as the thing worth keeping even after the mystical machinery underneath it is stripped out.

Press on what actually explains the good outcome if not accurate romantic instinct — perhaps that feeling-based choosers commit harder, or that the causal arrow runs backward (satisfaction retroactively generates the story of having 'known'), or that the sample of people who report success is filtered — and ask whether a true belief resting on a demonstrably false mechanism deserves the same trust, arriving at the observation that people have always said 'you'll know it when you feel it' but conclude that what's meant by knowing has to change even though the sentence stays exactly the same.

primary.axis: whether the popular defenses of a folk maxim ('choose the partner who feels right') are what actually make the maxim true
poles: the maxim is true because feeling is a reliable detector of compatibility
the maxim is true for reasons that have nothing to do with feeling being reliable at all

secondary.axis: whether exposing bad arguments for a belief should weaken our confidence in the belief itself
poles: bad reasons are parasitic and should be cut away without touching the conclusion
a conclusion propped up only by bad reasons has been quietly hollowed out and cannot be trusted the same way again

tension_system.interaction: the secondary tension is what stops the primary one from resolving neatly — because the essay refuses to say that removing the bad arguments leaves the belief intact, it cannot simply reassign the maxim a cleaner justification and move on

family_realization.note: Passage perfectly executes intent: separates 'conviction works' (survives audit) from 'instinct detects' (three alternative explanations). Difficulty is genuine—reader must hold both claims and feel the wedge.

ending_behavior.note: Final sentence narrows aperture precisely: 'knowing as a debt to be paid rather than a fact received.' Banality 'you'll know it' transforms from perceptual claim to moral commitment. Refusal suspended.

voice_consistency.note: Moral accountant voice: tallies commitment/narrative/filtering costs with quiet indignation. Slight unevenness—'the trouble is' and 'provided one hears' show human particularity. One concrete anchor: the church hall 1961.

distractor_efficiency.note: Q1(B) category_slip trap; Q2(A) missing_link trap; Q3(B) misreads tone; Q5(A) attacks wrong target; Q7(C) confuses self-report with evidence. All traps are genuinely tempting for strong readers misreading scope.

explanation_quality.note: Every wrong option names mechanism: premature_closure (Q1C), scope_inflation (Q2B), stage_misattribution (Q4B), causal_inversion (Q5D). All cite passage locations; no 'too extreme' or 'not mentioned' filler.

answers.reasoning: Passage's core split: advice survives, mechanism explanations don't.
Text explicitly says outcome survives while mechanism remains undecided.
Author separates outcome claim from perceptual/detection claim about feeling.
Text defines scanner as instrument tuned to detect suitability.
Filtering explanation confirmed would directly undermine survival of the outcome claim.
Advice works despite false justifications—separates efficacy from explanation.
Randomized manipulation producing same effect shows instinct isn't detecting real fit.
Text states studies would need decades and an unavailable control group.
